full_judgment:
4. In the writ petition, it was stated, inter alia, that on 23.06.1997 the petitioners along with five others filed an application before respondent No. 9, the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Jagannathpur, against respondent No. 10 and 9 (nine) others for reviewing an ex-parte order of mutation dated 04.06.1995 passed in Mutation Miscellaneous Case No. 70 of 1994-95 stating, inter alia, that they have been owning and possessing the land described in the schedule to the application in ejmali from their predecessor-in-interest and S.A. khatian was prepared correctly in their respective names. The petitioners have been cultivating Aman and Boro paddy in the scheduled land. On 23.06.1997 when the petitioners approached to pay rent, they were informed that respondent No. 10, Jamshed Mia and 9(nine) others had collusively mutated the land in their names, "by purposely manufactured papers and documents" without serving any notice upon them. The application gave rise to Miscellaneous Case No. 53 of 196-97(Review). Pursuant to the notice issued its the review application, respondent No. 10 appeared and prayed for adjournment and the case was fixed on 31.07.1997 for hearing, but before that date on 29.07.1997, respondent No. 10 filed Miscellaneous Case (Revision) No. 07 of 1997 before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Sunamaganj (respondent No. 6) against the aforesaid Miscellaneous Case No. 53/96-97(Review) and managed to get an order calling for the records from the office of respondent No. 9, the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Jagannathpur and an order of stay of further proceedings of the said review miscellaneous case. Respondent No. 10 tried to kill time on this or that plea and ultimately, the case was fixed for hearing on 23.11.1998. Meanwhile, respondent No. 10 filed another application on 27.08.1997 before respondent No. 5, the Deputy Commissioner, Sunamganj with the prayer for adding 9 (nine) acres of land or 48 plots of Patleechak mouza and 26 acres of land of 106 plots of Moizpur mouza, in total 35 acres of land, to Darikhanjanpur mouza. On 18.11.1997, the petitioners filed a written objection before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Sunamganj, respondent No. 6 opposing the prayer and stated in detail of the attempts of respondent No. 10 on different time for addition of certain plots from 2(two) different mouzas to be merged with Darikhanjanpur mouza. In the written objection, it was further stated that respondent No. 10 managed to serve notices upon the opposite parties of the case by forging their signatures in collusion with the process server, he managed to serve notice on Tara Mia who died in 1982, on Miajan and Kurpan Utah who died 40 years and 42 years respectively before filing the case and managed to obtain an ex-parte order on 04.06.1995 without serving any notice upon the petitioners and others. The office of respondent No. 5 rejected the said application for  addition of the said lands to Darikhanjanpur mouza by order dated 14.06.1998 considering the facts and circumstances of the case and all possible complicacies in respect of addition of the said two mouzas with Darikhanjanpur mouza. Respondent No. 10 again filed an application before respondent No. 5 for reviewing the said order dated 14.06.1998 which was also rejected by and under the signature of respondent No. 6 and communicated vide Office Memo SA 98/2352(2)1(3) dated 02.12.1998 in the said order, the respondent also discussed all possible complicacies of law8 and the reasons stated in the written objection filed by the petitioners and other as to the proposal of addition of the plots from two different mouzas with Darikhanjanpur. Against the said rejection, respondent No took an appeal before the Divisional Commissioner, Sylhet being Revenue Miscellaneous Appeal No. 288 of 1998 who by order dated 14.12.1998 stayed operation of the order of the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Sunamganj and in addition opined that "proposal shall go to survey, and Settlement Dept for final decision." Accordingly, respondent No. 4 by his order dated 25.07.1999 sent the case records to the Director General of Land Records and Surveys Directorate, Tejgaon, for taking necessary action. The clever respondent, in the meantime, managed to obtain an order from the office of respondent No. 1, Secretary, Ministry of Land under the signature of respondent No. 2 vide her office Memo No.  ভূঃমঃ/শ-২ (মৌঃ নাঃ পঃ)-৫/৯৯/৪৩৭ dated 27.08.2000 of the administrative approval for addition of said 9 acres of land of 48 plots of Patleechak mouza and 26 acres of land of 106 plots of Moizpur mouza with Darikhanjanpur mouza; hence, the petitioners filed the writ petition impugning the said memo. 

 5. It was further contended by way of submission that the office of respondent No. 1 "Passed administrative approval Notification" under the signature of respondent No. 2 vide her office Memo No.  ভূঃমঃ/শ-২ (মৌঃ নাঃ পঃ)-৫/৯৯/৪৩৭ dated 27.08.2000 without serving any notice upon the petitioners and was beyond jurisdiction as he was not empowered under rules 321 and 322 of the Bengal Survey and Settlement Manual, 1935(hereinafter referred to as the manual, 1935). The procedure laid down in rules 321 and 322 of the Manual, 1935 were also not complied with by respondent Nos. 1 and 2 before issuing the impugned notification. The application of respondent No. 10 for addition of some plots from two different mouzas with Darikhanjanpur mouza was rejected twice by the office of respondent No. 5 under the signature of respondent No. 6 after considering the facts and circumstances of the case against which respondent No. 10 did not approach the immediate higher authority, but taking the advantage of political influence managed to obtain an administrative approval in this regard from respondent Nos. 1 and 2 who approved the some beyond jurisdiction. Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 passed the order of approval without giving any opportunity of hearing to the petitioners and others. Moreover, respondent Nos. 1 and 2 were not the proper authorities under rules 321 and 322 of the manual, 1935 to give the administrative approval. Respondent Nos.1 and 2 passed the order of approval without taking into consideration of the facts and circumstances of the ease and the possible complicacy of laws where the Government will not be benefited, in any way, and will not cause any loss or injury to respondent No. 10, rather maps of three mouzas must be amended and the people of those three mouzas will suffer irreparable loss and injury about their record-of-rights, mutations, rents. In the present survey, the lands of those curtailed plots have been recorded under the previous Patleechak and Moizpur mouzas in the names of the petitioners and others by the survey authority and the attestation khatian has been prepared in their names, but respondent No. 10 did not raise any objection anywhere against such survey or attestation till today. The impugned order of approval was passed by the respondents for addition of certain plots from two different mouzas with Darikhanjanpur mouza on some unfounded, vague, illegal and arbitrary cause. The impugned notification was void, illegal, beyond jurisdiction and was the result of colourable exercise of power and as such, was liable to be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and was of no legal effect. 

 14. Mr. Qumrul Haque Siddique, who was appointed as amicus curiae, has filed a written submission. In his written submission, lie has given the history of the origin, meaning and legal basis of mouza, legal basis for fixing and re-fixing the exterior boundaries of mouza. He has tried to examine the legal status and force of the Manual, 1935. In connection with this, he has dealt with the English word `village', which bears similar meaning of the Bengali words 'Gram' or `Gaon'; he has also tried to trace back the history of settlements in villages right from the period of Menu, introduction of 'Soubha during the time of Akbar, the great Mughal Emperor, division of `Soubhas' of Bengal into the Circars or Sircars, the Circus into Purgunnas and the Purgunas into turfs, kismuts and villages or mouzas, the purpose   of creation of Village. The gradual history of `Khudkhast Rayot', that is, cultivators of lands residing in the same village, 'Paikast Raoyot', that is, those cultivating lands coining from nearby villages, the creation of Zemindars and the collection of rents by them from Raiyats through the instruments called `Sunnud' and to pay revenue to the royal treasury either directly or through Subedars, Dewans and Nahabs etc, the existence of some middle-interest-holders called Talukdars under the Zemindars, Talukdars who used to pay revenue to the Subcdars or Nawabs directly   like the Zemindars. The purchase of Talukdari of Calcutta, Sootanooty and Gobindpore by the East India Company in 1698, the acquisition of zemindary of 24 pergunnas by the said company as a grant on 23rd June, 1757, obtaining of grant of Dewani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa from Shah Alam, the emperor of Delhi on 12th August, 1765 by the East India Company, the collection of rent by the East India Company as rent collector; the decision of the East India Company on the 16th of August, 1767 to appoint Supervisors to superintendent the collection of rent and administration of justice; proclamation issued by the East India Company on 11th May, 1772 to form Revenue Council to take charge of the office of ,the Dewani, passing of Regulation on 14th May, 1772 to appoint Rent Farmers for 5 years for each pergunna, abolition of the post of Supervisors and the appointment of collectors as officers to collect rent and to prepare rent roll, making of settlements from 1777 to 1789 on yearly basis for collection of rent, abolition of Revenue Council on the 12th day of June, 1786 and in its place establishment of Board of Revenue, passing of Regulation for Decennial Settlement on the 10th February, 1790, direction upon the collectors to assess `Jumma' (amount or rent to be paid by the Zemindars) for their estates. Passing of Bengal Regulation No. 1 on 22nd March, 1793 providing for permanent settlement of estates to Zemindars and independent Talukdars at yearly Jumma assessed under the decennial settlement. Making provisions for preparing Quinquennial Register of Revenue paying estates in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa in which several particulars were to be recorded like present and future proprietors, 'jumma' etc by Regulation XLVII of 1793, preparation of Quinquennial registers and maintenance thereof mentioning Chauhaddi and Mouzas, undertaking survey   over whole of the permanently settled area in 1840 as an administrative measure which continued for 35 years, with the object to fix the outer boundaries or the topography of the different estates and mouzas. At the preliminary stages of such survey, boundary marks were fixed with mud-pillars commonly called Thaks and those recorded in the field hooks, field hooks were supplemented by a Roadad (Memorandum) and subsequently taking of more accurate and scientific survey called the Revenue Survey and preparation of maps accordingly. The enactment of the Survey Act, 1875 defining mouza as synonym of village, according to the said Act mouza included every village, hamlet, tola and similar subdivision of an estate, pergana or village by whatever name such subdivision may be known. The enactment of the Bengal Tenancy Act in 1885, shortly, 'the B.T. Act' with the principal object to give certain protection to the raiyats and the under Raiyats. So, mapping   of raiyati holdings and preparation of detailed record-of-rights became necessary. Chapter X of the B. T. Act made provisions   for preparation of record of rights. This Act did not take the term 'Mouza' instead it took the word 'village'. Section 3(19) of the B. T. Act defined 'village' as the area defined, surveyed and recorded as a distinct and separate village in the general land revenue survey which has been made of the province of Bengal, or any survey made by the Government which has been adopted by notification in the Calcutta or Eastern Bengal or Assam Gazette or which may he adopted by notification as the Calcutta Gazette as defining village for the purpose of this clause in any specified area; and, where a survey has not been made by, or under the authority of the Government, such area as the Collector may, with the sanction of the Board of Revenue, by general or special order, declare to constitute a village provided that, when an order has been made under section 101 directing that a survey be made and a record-of-rights prepared in respect of any local area, estate, tenure or part thereof, the Government may, by notification in the Calcutta  Gazette declare that in such local area, estate. tenure or part thereof "village" shall mean the area which for the purposes of such survey and record-of-rights may he adopted by the Revenue Officer with the sanction of the Board of Revenue accorded under the provisions of section 115A as the unit of survey and record. 

 16. It has further been submitted by Mr. Siddique that The East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (hereinafter   referred to as the Act, 1950) which was passed by the East Bengal Legislative Assembly, after assent of the Governor General as Act, XXVIII of 1951 was published   in the Dacca Gazette on the 16th May, 1951, the Act has provided provisions for acquisition of all rent receiving interest, preparation of fresh rent roll, compensation assessment roll and fresh record-of-rights. Section 17 has authorized the Government to make an order for preparation of such record-of-rights. Section 18 has provided for prescribing the particulars to be included in such record-of-rights and section 18 has provided for draft publication, objection, appeal and final publication of such record-of-rights. He has also pointed out that the State Acquisition Rules, 1951 were framed under Part-IV. Rules 17 to 38 of Chapter-IV of the said Rules have provided for preparation and publication of record-of-rights and procedure for traverse survey and Cadastral survey have been provided therein. 

 17. Mr. Siddique has further pointed out that sections 32 to 46 in Chapter-V of the Act, 1950 have provided for preparation of compensation assessment roll and acquisition of rent receiving interests. Section 46 has provided for modification of the record-of-rights prepared under Chapter-IV by eliminating the entire chain of interest or rent receivers and then for reprint and distribution of the record-of-rights. Section 144 and subsequently added section 144A (inserted by amendment, 1967) of the Act in Part-V, Chapter XVII has provided for revision of the record-of-rights and a presumption of correctness has been attached to the revised record-of-rights. Section 152 has empowered the Government to make rules for Part-V. He has further pointed out that in exercise of power under section 152 of the Act, 1950 the Tenancy Rules, 1954 (hereinafter referred to as the Rules, 1954), was framed. Section 144 of the Act, 1950 has given power to the Government to make an order to prepare or revise the record-o f-rights in accordance with the Rules. Chapter-VI consisting of rules 26-35 of the Rules, 1954 has provided detailed procedure for revision of record-of-rights, rules 27 and 27A thereof have laid down almost the same procedure as was made by rule 49 of the Rules made under the B.T. Act. 

 20. Mr. Siddique has lastly submitted that record-of-rights prepared under Part IV of the Act, 1950 for the entire of present Bangladesh was finally published by 1962-63 and in Sylhet, in 1963. In 1967, by amendment section 143A was inserted in the Act, 1950 which was repealed in 1975. In section 143A, provision was made for applying to the civil Court for correction of the record-of-rights under Part-IV. It further makes the legislative intent clear that once a record-of-rights is finally published, it goes Out of the administrative/executive domain of the Government, to alter it. Only a pronouncement by the Court can say whether it was correct or wrong. Section 80 in Part- V of the Act says that from the date of coming into force of Part-V, the enactments specified in the schedule shall be repealed. The schedule shows that both the B. T. Act and the Sylhet Tenancy Act, 1936 along with several other statutes have been repeated. The present case has arisen out of a boundary dispute of three mouzas under police station-Jagannathpur within district-Sunamganj, it was in the district of Sylhet till 1984 and Sylhet was not a part of Bengal before partition of India in 1947. Rather it was a part of Assam. The Assam Land and Revenue Regulation was passed in 1886. The Sylhet Tenancy Act was enacted in 1936. Provisions lie survey and preparation of record-of-rights were also there. But no survey was made and no record-of-rights was prepared there before the Act, 1950 came into operation, as was done in the rest of Bangladesh. Mauza map prepared in the greater Sylhet district in course of preparation of the record-of-rights as ordered under section 17 of the Act, 1950 became final with final publication of the record-of-rights (S.A. Khatian) in 1963. The executive branch of the Government lost all of its administrative powers to alter/correct/modify the map and the record-of-rights finally published in 1963. In between 1967 to 1975, r the civil Courts were vested with limited power to direct correction of finally published record-of-rights. But that did not include correction/alteration of exterior boundary of a mouza. Rules 1 and 2 of the Manual, 1935 state that it is a compilation of the principal rules of procedure relating to surveys and settlements. Survey and settlement operations or survey operations alone are/were conducted under different Regulations and Acts. But the rules of procedure   and the technical rules relate primarily to surveys and settlements under the Settlement Laws, the B. T. Act and the Bengal Survey Act. Thus it is clear that the rules of the Manual, 1935 do not have; force of law. Rule 321 or 322 or any other rule of the said Manual does not authorise the Government to alter the exterior boundaries of any mouza shown in the S.A. map after final publication of S.A. khatian in 1962-63. Now, Part-V of the Act, 1950 having already come into effect the Government has power under section 144 thereof to make an order to prepare or revise the record-of-rights for any area of such an order is made, than and then, only Settlement Officer can start a proceeding under rule 27A of the Rules, 1954 (1955) for alteration of the exterior boundary of a mouza strictly following the requirements of that rule and a successful completion of the process would permit preparation of a new mouza map including or excluding any land which was not there in the S.A. map of that mouza. Any other action to change exterior boundary limits of any mouza like the present one is without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. 

 25. From the findings of the high Court Division as summarized hereinbefore, it is apparent that the learned Judges did not, at all, dwell on any disputed question of fact. The facts considered by the learned Judges as mentioned hereinbefore/ were not disputed by the contesting writ-respondent in his affidavit-in-opposition filed before the High Court Division. In the leave petition as well as in the concise statement, the only fact disputed is that in 1972, the Board of Revenue was abolished, so there was no need of concurrence of the Board of Land Revenue to conclude the proceedings initiated by the respondent as observed by the High Court Division and this is a mixed question of fact and law and it need not be, at all, gone into in the context. In fact, the High Court Division declared the impugned administrative approval vide annexure-F to the writ petition to have been issued without lawful authority mainly considering the provision of rules 321 and 322 of the Manual, 1935 and rule 27A (2) of the 15, Rules, 1954(55) with reference to the particular fact that the whole proceeding was initiated by an individual. Furthermore, from a reading of the writ petition, it appears that of paragraphs 3-19, 3-11 are statements of facts and 12-19 are the sub-missions which are usually made by the learned Advocate of the writ-petitioners. Again, from the statements made in paragraphs 3-11, it appears that the statements made in paragraph-4 to the effect that on 23.06.1997 while the petitioners pi approached to pay rent, they were informed that respondent No. 10 and 9(nine) others had collusively mutated the lands in their names by manufactured papers and documents without serving any The notice upon them and in paragraph-7 that in the written objection filed before respondent No. 6, they stated that respondent No. 9 managed to serve notices upon the opposite parties of the Mutation Miscellaneous Case No. 70 of 1994-95 in collusion with the process server and managed to serve notice of the case on Tara Miah who died in 1982, on Miajan and Kurpan Ullah who died 40 years and 42 years respectively before filing the case and managed to obtain an ex-parte order on 04.06.1995 appear to as to be a bit disputed, but those facts have no bearing on the proceeding in question in which the impugned administrative approval was given inasmuch as those facts related to the said miscellaneous mutation case in which the respondent along with 9(nine) others obtained an ex-parte order of mutation only and that has nothing to do with the correction of mouza map/change of mouza map of the 3( three) mouzas, namely Patleechak, Moizpur and Darikbanjanpur mouzas as prayed for by the respondent. So, we find no substance in the first submission on which leave was granted. 

 28. There is no dispute that after whole-sale acquisition of the rent receiving interests with effect from the 14th April, 1956 including the Sylhet District (till 1984 Sunamganj was part of the Sylhet District), preparation of fresh rent roll, compensation assessment roll and fresh record-of-rights was required. Chapter-IV, Part-IV of the Act, 1950 has provided for preparation of record-of-rights and section 17 has authorized the Government to make an order for preparation of such record-of-rights. Section 18 of the Act, 1950 has provided for prescribing the particulars to be included in such record-of-rights and section 19 has provided for draft publication, objection, appeal and final publication of such record-of-rights. Rules were framed under Part- IV called the State Acquisition Rule, 1951. Chapter-IV of the said Rules consisting rules 17-38 has provided for preparation and publication of record-of-rights. Sections 32 to 46 in Chapter-V of the Act, 1950 have provided fine preparation of compensation assessment roll and acquisition of rent receiving interests. Section 46 of the Act, 1950 has provided for modification of the record-of-rights prepared under Chapter-IV by eliminating the entire chain of interest of rent receivers and then for reprint and distribution of the record-of-rights. Part II Chapter II, Part III Chapter III, Part IV, Chapters VA, VI to X1 of the Act, 1950 are with regard to acquisition of rent receiving interests and for payment, of compensation for such acquisition. Sections 81 to 143 of the Act have dealt with class, status, right and liabilities of tenants, enhancement and reduction of rents, collection and realisation of rent, subdivision and amalgamation holdings and maintenance of Record of rights. Section 144 of the Act and subsequently added section 144A (inserted by amendment, 1967) are in Part- V. Chapter-XVII in Part-V of the Act has provided for maintenance and revision of the record-of-rights and a presumption of correctness has been attached to the revised record-o rights. Section 152 has empowered the: Government to make rules for Part-V and in exercise of the said power the Rules, 1954 was framed. It is also pertinent to mention that Chapters l-IV of the Rules, 1954 were published in the Dacca Gazette on 7th April, 1955 and Chapters V-IX of the Rules were published in the Dacca Gazette on 14th August, 1955. 

 30. Rules 1 and 2 of the Manual, 1935 have clearly stated that it is a compilation of the principal rules of procedure relating to surveys and settlements. Survey and settlement operations or survey operations alone are/week conducted under different Regulations and Acts. But the rules of procedure and the technical rules relate primarily to surveys and settlements under the Settlement Laws, the B.T. Act and the Bengal Survey Act. Thus, it is clear that the rules of the Manual, 1935 cannot over-ride   or supersede the laws, namely: the Act, 1950 and the Rules, 1954(55). Consequently, rules 321 and 322 or any other rule(s) of the said Manual does not authorize the Government to alter the exterior boundaries of any mouza shown in the S.A. map after final publication of the S.A. khatian in 1962-63. And if an order is made under section 144 of the Act, 1950, to prepare or revise the record-of-rights for any area, then and then, only Settlement Officer can start a proceeding under rule 27A of the Rules, 1954(55) for alteration of the exterior boundary of a mouza strictly following the requirements of that Rules and a successful completion of the process would permit preparation of a new mouza map including or excluding only land which was not there in S.A. map of that mouza. Any other action to change the exterior boundary limits of any mouza shall be without lawful authority and is of no legal effect as rightly submitted by Mr. Siddique. 

 36. From this letter of the Director General, Land Records and Surveys, it is clear that without starting any proceeding of as provided in rule 321 of the Manual, 1935 and submission of any proposal by the Assistant Settlement Officer to the Zonal Settlement Officer for correction of the mouza map/change of mould map as mandated in rule 27(2) of the Rules, 1954, report was given by the Assistant Settlement Officer for correction of the mouza map of the said 3(three) mouzas. A so-called "attending sheet" showing that 100 villagers were present on 29.05.1997 in an apparently inquiry held by the Chairman of No. 2 Patlecchak Union Parishad regarding the correction of the mouza map/change of mouza map of the mouzas in question has been quilted in the body of the affidavit-in-opposition. In the so-called "attending sheet" quoted in the body of the affidavit-in-opposition except the name and father's name of 100 people, no other particulars, such as, village or mouza has been mentioned. It further appears from a notice quoted in the body of the affidavit-in-opposition that the Chairman of the said Union Parishad issued the same on 01.06.1997 asking the people of Moizpur and Patleechak (not Darikhanjanpur) to remain present at Rasulganj Bazar on 03.06.1997 at 12 O'clock with their respective papers for Molding a meeting to decide "about the correction of mouza map/change of mouza map." At the bottom of the notice, names of 3(three) persons each of Patleechak mouza and Moizpur mouza without disclosing their full identities, such as, father's name, have been mentioned. The notice further shows that the same was issued at the instance of the Assistant Settlement Officer, Jagannathpur who earlier gave his report in favour of correction of the mouza wap/change of mouza map. No fact was "stated in the affidavit-in-opposition and no other particular was furnished as to how the said notice was served upon the inhabitants/residents of the said two villages/mouzas. It is also very significant to note that prior to the issuance of the said notice for holding enquiry on the subject, the Chairman had allegedly enquired into the matter on 29.05.1997 as sought to be proved by the "attending sheet" as stated hereinbefore. So the notice, even if issued on 01.06.1997, does not, at all, show that Amy enquiry was held to ascertain the opinions of the local people within the meaning of rule 27A(2) of the Rules, 1954 read with rule 321 of the Manual, 1935. In this regard, it is to the noted that law does not recognize any such exercise by the Chairman of any Union Parishad. 

 42. It is very pertinent to state that the opinions mentioned by the Assistant Settlement Officer in his order dated 25.04.1999 and as mentioned while stating the case of the respondent, were given by the concerned persons at a time when no proceeding by way of starting a miscellaneous   case as required by rule 321 of the Manual, 1935 was, at all, started. This fact is also evident from the letter written by Director General, and Records and Surveys Directorate to the Zonal Settlement Officer on 16.03.1997 vide his Memo No. 66/90/510 and the letter written by the Zonal Settlement Officer, Sylhet Zone to the Deputy Commissioner, Sunamganj vide Memo No.  ৩৩/২৯/পিঃ ৮৩৪ dated 15.06.1999. From the said letter of the Zonal Settlement Officer written to the Deputy Commissioner, Sunamganj and his subsequent letter dated 05.08.1999 vide Memo No. 33/29/P:/1098 written to the Director General, Land Records and Surveys, it is apparent that the miscellaneous case was started only in 1999. From the Memo of the Zonal Settlement Officer, it further appears that a fresh application was filed by the respondent on 22.02.1999 allegedly on behalf of the local people (এলাকাবাসীর পক্ষে) for severing 9.00 acres Of lands of 48 plots of Patleechak mouza and 26:00 acres of lands of Moizpur Monza and to add those with Darikhanjanpur mouza, but in law as discussed above, there was no scope of filing such application. The said Memo of the Zonal Settlement Officer further reveals that the miscellaneous case was initiated on the basis of the so-called reports of the local administration which were obtained or given much prior to the starting of the same and that too without completing the hearing of the concerned persons and the people of the locality as stated in order dated 25.04.1999 of the Assistant Settlement Officer. And it is also a tact that no formal proposal on the subject in compliance with the provisions of rule 27A (2) of the Rules, 1954 was submitted by the Assistant Settlement Officer. In this regard, it is also necessary to keep on record that only after the starting of the said miscellaneous case opinion was sought for from the Superintendent of Police, Sunamganj by the Zonal  Settlement Officer by his Memo No. 33/29/P:/1097 dated 05.08.1999 who gave his report on 03.10.1999 (after the letter to the Director General, Land Records and Surveys was sent by the Zonal Settlement Officer on (15.08.1999) in a casual manner without giving his own independent opinion just' saying that necessary action might be taken on the basis of the report of the Thana Nirbahi Officer, the Assistant Commissioner(Land) and the Chairman of the Union Parishad. That the Zonal Settlement Officer acted on the application of an individual, the respondent in clear defiance of law as discussed above is clear from his letter dated 15.06.1999 written to the Deputy Commissioner, Sunamganj vide his Memo No. 33/29/P:/834 as quoted herein below. 

 50. The proceeding of Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 1999 was not produced before the High Court Division and no date is also available from the record as to its initiation, but obviously the case was not initiated before 1999. It is also apparent from the order of the Assistant Settlement Officer dated 25.04.1999 that after the miscellaneous case was started, no attempt was made to lake the opinions of the people of the 3(three) mouzas who would be the most affected persons in case the mouza map is changed/corrected. From the said order, it is also apparent that there was heavy tadbir from the respondent to get the job done any how and this further shows that the concerned functionaries did not give their opinions on the application of the respondent independently in accordance with rule 321 of the Manual, 1935 and rule 27A (2) of the Rules, 1954(55). It is also pertinent to state at the risk of repetition that in the meantime, the respondent's application filed to the Deputy Commissioner, Sunamganj on 27.08.1997 for addition of 9.00 acres and 26.00 acres of lands of Patleechak and Moizpur mouza respectively with Darikhanjanpur mouza was rejected on 14.06.1998; application filed by the respondent for reviewing the said order was also rejected on (12.12.1998 against which he filed Revenue Miscellaneous Appeal No. 288 of 1998 before the Divisional Commissioner, Sylhet who without disposing of the said revenue miscellaneous appeal on merit sent the records to the Director General, Land Records and Surveys for final decision relying on the submission of the learned Advocate for the respondent that the issue had been pending for final decision by the Survey and Settlement Department, but from the correspondences of the Assistant Settlement Officer, the Zonal Settlement Officer and the Director General, Land Records and Surveys, it does not appear that the fact of rejection of the prayer of the respondent adding 9.00 acres of lands of Patleechak mouza and 26.00 acres of lands of Moizpur mouza with Darikhanjanpur mouza by the Deputy Commissioner was, at all, noticed. The High Court Division, in deciding the merit of the Rule, took notice of this fact of rejection of respondent's prayer twice by the highest local authority. The High Court Division further noticed that only the Chairman of Patleechak Union Parishad informed the Thana Nirbahi Officer that the people had no objection if the said lands were added with Darikhanjanpur mouza and on such report the Zonal Settlement Officer, the Thana Nirbahi Officer, the Additional Deputy Commissioner and the Superintendent of Police acted. From the various reports and the inter sc correspondences amongst the concerned functionaries as discussed above, we also find substances in the finding of the High Court Division that “There is no dispute that in the process the opinion of the people of village ‘Moizpur’ or ‘Darkhanjanpur’ (sic) was never sought for.”
